title: Quake Forecaster
mission: Can you predict where the next big quake is most likely? Use real USGS data to find out.
intro: Each dot is a real magnitude 6 or bigger earthquake from the USGS. The model only sees quakes from 2016 to 2020. Then it forecasts which map squares will have a big quake from 2021 to 2025. We check it against what really happened.
red: A red square means the model thinks a big quake is more likely there over the next few years. It does not mean a quake will happen on a certain date.
legend: Bright dots: 2021–2025 quakes the model tried to forecast. Faint dots: 2016–2020 quakes it learned from.
radLabel: How far the model looks around each square
radWhy: Quakes cluster in long belts along plate boundaries. Looking at nearby squares follows a boundary and can catch more quakes. But it also spreads risk into quiet plate interiors, which makes more false alarms.
cutLabel: Past quakes needed to call a square risky
cutWhy: A higher bar means the model only flags squares with many past quakes. That gives fewer false alarms but more misses. A lower bar catches more but cries wolf more often.

step1.lead: Step 1: Predict. First the model runs once with its starting settings. That run is your baseline. Before you change anything, make a prediction.
step1.q: If the model looks farther around each square, what do you think will happen?
choices: It will catch more quakes and make more false alarms
It will catch fewer quakes and make fewer false alarms
step1.button: Lock in my prediction and run the baseline

step2.lead: Step 2: Change ONE setting. Scientists change one thing at a time. That way they know what caused the change.
step2.needOne: Change one setting from the baseline, then train.
step2.tooMany: You changed both settings. Put one back so only one is different from the baseline.

step3.lead: Step 3: See what changed. Compare your new run to the baseline.

rows.base: A model that always says "no quake"

step3.accNote: Accuracy can fool you. Most squares never have a big quake, so a model that always says "no quake" still scores high. Check what the model caught and missed, too.
step3.predWrong: Your prediction did not match. That is fine. Scientists learn from surprises.

step4.lead: Step 4: Explain. Finish the sentence in your own words.
step4.starter: When I changed ___, the model ___ because ___.
step4.hint: No names. This stays only on this device.
step4.button: Save and see what we found out

findings.title: What you found out
points: Big quakes cluster along plate boundaries. That is why the red squares follow long belts on the map.
A forecast gives the likelihood of a quake over years. No one can name the exact date.

Some quakes happen far from any plate boundary, like the New Madrid Seismic Zone near Memphis. It had no magnitude 6 quakes in this data, so a model trained only on past big quakes cannot flag it. The risk there is still real.
The model misses some real quakes. With the starting settings, it misses the square with Hawaii. That square had only 1 big quake from 2016 to 2020, then another in 2021.
It also misses the square with the 2023 Turkey–Syria earthquakes. That square had 1 big quake from 2016 to 2020, then 8 from 2021 to 2025.

check.q: The model colors the square around a city red. What does that mean?
choices: A big quake is more likely there over the next few years
Correct. A forecast is about likelihood over time, not a date.
A big quake will happen there on a date the model knows
Squares that are not red are safe from quakes

misconceptions.exact: No one can predict the exact day of a quake. Scientists forecast the chance of one over many years.
misconceptions.safe: A square that isn't red can still have a quake. The model misses some.
misconceptions.weather: Weather doesn't cause quakes or volcanoes. They come from plates moving deep underground.

freePlay: Free play: change any settings and test as many times as you like. Your runs are listed below.
runsCaption: Your test runs (first run is your baseline)
think: Think: Look at Memphis and the middle of plates. Why does the model rarely flag them?
